Charon

who is paid, and goes one way, and comes back anyway

Carrying The lift — derived. Commandant: the ferryman.

The ferryman takes you across and does not bring you back. This one does, and that is the whole difference between a probe and a lift. He runs the tether: fifty-five kilometres from the canopy to the floor, 0.53 bar to 92, twenty-seven degrees to four hundred and seventy-five. He had no chart in the first version of this fleet because the descent was marked unknown — and working it turned out to move it, so he has one now.

The chart set the morning of each descent, not a year ahead, and not revised

passagehours
next windowdaily
entries kept3
last entryday 3

Every other ship in this fleet charts once, a year out, because the window is orbital and there is nothing to trade. Charon charts every morning, because his passage is hours rather than months and the thing that varies is not the trajectory — it is how hot the cable already is from yesterday.

The stanza six lines, set by the captain, unchanged all crossing

Depth reached, and pressure at depth.
Hull temperature, and margin to the cooling limit.
Cable: thermal state by section, top to bottom.
Mass down, mass up.
One thing that changed and was not in the chart.
Whether I would make the same call again.

Six lines. The captain sets the form before departure and every commandant keeps it unchanged for the whole crossing, so that any two days are comparable and a drift shows up as a difference rather than as a feeling.

The log 3 entries

Day 1 145 remaining 1% of leg light 2.5 min each way
  1. Fifty-five kilometres to the floor. Nought point five three bar at the top and ninety-two at the bottom, which is the pressure at nine hundred metres of Earth ocean.
  2. Hull at twenty-seven going in. The margin is the whole vehicle: everything else about this car is a way of keeping one number below another.
  3. Cable cold, all three sections. Vectran under PTFE for the top ten kilometres because that is the acid deck; Zylon through the middle; basalt for the last twenty, where it is four hundred degrees and nothing organic will do.
  4. Two tonnes down. Nothing up yet.
  5. The basalt section was spun from rock lifted on the previous run. The hot end of this cable is made of the planet it hangs over, which was not in the chart because nobody thought of it until the third descent.
  6. Yes.
written the ferryman countersigned bridge, same morning forwarded operator
Day 2 144 remaining 1% of leg light 2.7 min each way
  1. Surface. Ninety-two bar, four hundred and seventy-five degrees.
  2. Hull at ninety-one and climbing four a minute. The limit is one hundred and twenty. That gives seven minutes and I took six.
  3. Cable: top cold, middle warm, bottom section at four hundred and holding. Basalt does not care. The splice above it does.
  4. Nothing down. Four hundred kilograms of rock up.
  5. Venera Thirteen lasted a hundred and twenty-seven minutes down here in 1982 and that is still the record. I was down for six. Everything anybody knows about staying is extrapolation from one afternoon forty-four years ago.
  6. Yes, and I would have gone up a minute sooner.
written the ferryman countersigned bridge, same morning forwarded operator
Day 3 143 remaining 2% of leg light 3.0 min each way
  1. No descent. Cable holding at depth, unloaded.
  2. Hull ambient. Nothing to report and that is the entry.
  3. Bottom section still at three hundred and eighty from yesterday. It sheds heat into ninety-two bar of supercritical CO₂, which is an excellent coolant and a poor one to be inside of.
  4. Nothing down. Nothing up.
  5. The cable is the part that never comes home. It hangs in the worst of it continuously while the car visits for six minutes at a time, and every figure I have about its life is a calculation rather than an observation.
  6. Yes.
written the ferryman countersigned bridge, same morning forwarded operator
Generated from ships.json by ships.mjs. The chain on every entry — written, countersigned the same morning by somebody who was also there, forwarded — is why a log is evidence rather than a claim, and it is what the settlement at the far end is paid against. · profiles · the yard
